en: During the day, land heats up faster than the ocean, causing warm air over land to rise and cooler ocean air to rush in as a sea breeze.
As altitude increases on Mount Pulag, atmospheric pressure decreases, causing the air temperature to drop and creating a colder climate.
When tree roots grow into rock cracks, they expand and exert physical pressure, eventually breaking the solid rock apart into smaller soil particles.
When hot magma from beneath the Earth's crust cools and solidifies, its minerals crystallize to form hard, solid igneous rocks like granite.
Plant roots absorb groundwater, which travels up the stem and evaporates through leaf pores, adding water vapor to the atmosphere during transpiration.
Because Earth's axis is tilted, different hemispheres receive varying amounts of direct sunlight as the planet orbits the Sun, causing the seasons.
Extreme pressure and temperature in the Sun's core force hydrogen atoms to fuse into helium, releasing massive amounts of light and heat energy.
The Moon's gravitational pull exerts a stronger force on the ocean water facing it, pulling the water into a bulge that creates high tides.
When tectonic plates get stuck at their edges, stress builds up until the rocks suddenly break and slip, releasing energy as an earthquake.
When the Sun heats the ground, warm moist air rapidly rises and cools, causing water vapor to condense into cumulonimbus clouds that produce thunderstorms.
When liquid seawater evaporates into water vapor, it leaves dissolved salts behind, which is why the ocean remains salty despite continuous evaporation.
Fungi and bacteria secrete enzymes that break down dead plant leaves, transforming the organic matter into nutrient-rich, dark brown soil material called humus.
